deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivations, formulas or computations. It is a sequence of six aphorisms or methodological notes, separated by horizontal rules, of the kind Hilbert collected in this notebook (the previous and next pages are of the same type).

(1) Number theory is praised as the field in which mathematical concepts flow from the clearest sources. Perhaps nothing even outside mathematics satisfies the mind as much as the construction of the theory of algebraic number fields (Zahlkörpertheorie). This echoes the preface of Hilbert's Zahlbericht (1897).

(2) Anecdote attributed to Hensel. A scientific paper that lacks the main thing needed to reach its goal is like someone telling Helmholtz he has 'almost' discovered the perpetuum mobile. All he still lacks is a little thing that keeps going back and forth. In other words, the missing piece is exactly the impossible core.

(3) A second anecdote 'nach Hensel'. Reducing one difficulty to another is like a surgeon who, after a very difficult and dangerous operation, moves the hunchback's hump from the left side to the right.

(4) Only through the axiomatic method does mathematics rise from a 'science of calculation' to true philosophical height. The axiomatic method must, however, be understood correctly and generally, as including existence and uniqueness proofs. This programmatic theme continues on the next page (consistency and independence; the axiomatic way as the 'Königsweg' to mathematical physics) and anticipates 'Axiomatisches Denken' (1918).

(5) Goethe's 'Himmelhoch jauchzend, zum Tode betrübt' (Klärchen's song in Egmont) fits the creative thinker well. He believes he has found something, then sees again that it does not work.

(6) A teaching principle, apparently a draft remark for a lecture. Hilbert will give the audience the best and sharpest methods at once. A modern soldier likewise does not first learn to shoot with a crossbow but is handed the most modern repeating rifle straight away.

There is nothing to reconstruct in modern notation.

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only aphorisms and methodological remarks, with no mathematics. Their content matches views Hilbert is well known to have held: the Zahlbericht preface on number theory and the axiomatic method as later stated in 1918. Notebook aphorisms of this kind (including the Königsweg passage on the next page) have been quoted by historians such as Rowe and Corry. The two Hensel anecdotes are charming but historically minor.
